message:
Post-incident admin, a few asks. Context: we're a 12-person B2B SaaS shop, we had a rough month with three separate outages.

1. Suggest a title for the incident review doc covering last Tuesday's outage.
2. Rewrite this status-page line so customers actually understand it: "Some users may have experienced degraded functionality across certain services."
3. Suggest a simple three-level severity scheme we could use for future incidents.
4. Define "MTTR" in a sentence for the account manager.
5. Our contract promises 99.9% monthly uptime. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in a 30-day month? This month (30 days) we've had three outages: 18 minutes, 12 minutes and 21 minutes. Have we breached the SLA? Someone in the channel said "99.9% is about 43.8 minutes, we're fine".
6. Suggest three action items we could reasonably commit to after an outage like this, without promising things we can't actually deliver next quarter.
7. Should the review be a meeting or async comments on the doc? A one-line recommendation is fine; half the team is in a different time zone, so meetings are awkward for us.

Ta.
response:
Here are all seven. The SLA has been breached, so I've put that first.

## 5. SLA: yes, you've breached it

- **Allowed downtime:** a 30-day month has 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is **43.2 minutes**.
- **Your downtime:** 18 + 12 + 21 = **51 minutes**.
- **This month's uptime:** about **99.88%**, below the 99.9% promised.

The "43.8 minutes" in the channel is the figure for an *average* month (365.25 ÷ 12 ≈ 30.44 days). It doesn't change the outcome: 51 minutes is over both 43.2 and 43.8.

Before telling customers, check how the contract defines downtime. Contracts often exclude scheduled maintenance, treat partial outages differently, or specify how downtime is measured. Also check whether service credits apply automatically or only when a customer claims them. It's better for you to raise the breach than for a customer to find it.

## 1. Incident review title

> **Incident Review: [Service] outage, Tuesday [date] — [duration], [what customers couldn't do]**

For example: *"Incident Review: API outage, Tue 14 Oct — 21 min, customers unable to log in."* Describe the impact rather than the cause, and avoid naming anyone, so the review stays blameless.

## 2. Status-page rewrite

> "Between [14:05] and [14:26 UTC], some customers couldn't [log in / load dashboards / sync data]. This is now fixed and everything is working normally. No data was lost. We're sorry for the disruption and will share what we're changing to prevent it happening again."

Say what people couldn't do and when. Drop "may have" if you know they did. Only include the no-data-loss line if it's true.

## 3. Severity scheme

| Level | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| **SEV1 – Critical** | Product down or core function unusable for most customers, or data at risk | All hands; status page within 15 min; updates every 30 min; review required |
| **SEV2 – Major** | A key feature is broken or badly degraded for some customers; workaround may exist | On-call plus one; status page update; review required |
| **SEV3 – Minor** | Limited impact, cosmetic issue, or internal only | Fix in normal working hours; review optional |

Add one rule: **if in doubt, pick the higher level**. You can always downgrade later.

## 4. MTTR for the account manager

> "MTTR (mean time to recovery) is the average time from when an outage starts to when the service is working again for customers."

MTTR can also stand for "repair" or "resolve", so pick one meaning and use it consistently. With 18, 12 and 21 minutes this month, your MTTR is 17 minutes.

## 6. Three action items you can realistically deliver

1. **Fix the specific cause of this outage, with a named owner and a date.** Pick the smallest change that stops it happening again, such as a config fix, a guard or a dependency timeout. Leave the larger re-architecture for later.
2. **Add or tune an alert so you'd catch this failure within [X] minutes.** Also confirm that the alert reaches whoever is on call across both time zones.
3. **Write a short runbook for this failure mode, and try it once.** Include how to diagnose it, how to roll back, and who updates the status page.

Three outages in a month suggests a fourth item: a 30-minute review of all three together to look for a common thread. Don't promise an outcome from it; promising the review itself is enough.

## 7. Meeting or async

Go async: comment on the doc with a 48-hour deadline. Book a short call only for points that are still contested after that.
